analysis.one_liner: Repeals a list of federal subsidies, including sugar price supports and regional development agencies.
analysis.headline: A bill to end the sugar price support program and shut down two federal development agencies was referred to six House committees and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Mick Mulvaney (R-SC) introduced this bill in April 2013 to roll back what he called outdated federal subsidies. The largest single target was the federal sugar program, which keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels through price supports and import limits — a program whose main beneficiaries are sugar growers and whose main cost falls on food companies and consumers. The bill would also terminate the Appalachian Regional Commission and the Economic Development Administration, agencies that send grants to economically distressed rural and urban communities, and end federal loan guarantees for railroad improvement projects. After being referred to six House committees and three subcommittees, the bill saw no hearings, no markup, and no vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed: consumers and taxpayers. The sugar program works by guaranteeing growers a high price through government loans and by restricting imports, which raises the price of sugar (and sugar-containing foods) above world market levels for American shoppers. Ending it would lower those prices and stop taxpayers from backing the sugar loan program. Taxpayers would also stop funding the Appalachian Regional Commission, the Economic Development Administration, and railroad loan guarantees. However, residents of distressed Appalachian and rural communities who rely on ARC and EDA grants for local jobs and infrastructure would lose a source of federal investment.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the sugar price support and production adjustment program, which keeps U.S. sugar prices above world levels and passes those higher costs to consumers and food buyers.

Terminates the Appalachian Regional Commission and the Economic Development Administration and repeals the Public Works and Economic Development Act of 1965, ending federal grant programs and the taxpayer spending behind them.
Ends federal loan guarantees for railroad rehabilitation and improvement projects and the Secretary's authority for railroad safety research and development programs.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed: sugar growers, who would lose the price support program that shields them from world prices; local governments and development organizations in distressed Appalachian and rural communities that receive ARC and EDA grants; and railroad projects that counted on federal loan guarantees. Workers in communities dependent on those federal development dollars would bear the loss locally.

drawbacks.text: Terminating the Appalachian Regional Commission and the Economic Development Administration would cut federal investment in some of the country's poorest regions; these agencies fund job training, water and sewer systems, and business development in towns that often cannot finance such projects themselves.
Ending railroad loan guarantees and safety research programs could slow rail improvement projects and reduce federal investment in rail safety.
The bill took a single up-or-down approach to a long list of programs, so members who wanted to keep, say, EDA but cut the sugar program had no way to vote for part of it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixed a clear consumer win with real local losses. Dismantling the sugar program would have saved consumers and taxpayers money, since the program's costs are spread across millions of shoppers while its benefits go to a concentrated group of growers. But shutting down ARC and EDA would have withdrawn federal money from poor communities with few other funding sources, and there was no plan to redirect that support. A more targeted bill — cutting the sugar subsidy without eliminating regional development aid — would have weighed more clearly on the consumer side.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in six House committees and three subcommittees for the rest of the Congress without a hearing or a vote, and expired when the session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mick Mulvaney (R-SC) introduced the bill on April 15, 2013, with 11 Republican cosponsors.

The House referred it to six committees — Transportation and Infrastructure, Ways and Means, Agriculture, Natural Resources, Financial Services, and Armed Services — which split it across subcommittees on economic development, fisheries, and trade.
No committee ever reported the bill, no floor vote was held, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill.
The sugar price support program, ARC, EDA, and the railroad loan guarantees the bill targeted all remained in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, sugar growers kept their price support program, and the Appalachian Regional Commission and the Economic Development Administration kept operating and funding distressed communities. Taxpayers and consumers gained nothing that the bill would have delivered.

for.name: Rep. Mick Mulvaney
for.role: Sponsor; introduced the bill to repeal the sugar price support program, terminate ARC and EDA, and end railroad loan guarantees
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 11 Republican cosponsors

for.name: 11 Republican cosponsors
for.role: Original supporters of the repeal bill

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee (Chair Bill Shuster)
against.role: Primary committee of referral; never scheduled a markup or hearing
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after the April 2013 referral, leaving the bill unreported through the end of the Congress

against.name: Five other House committees of referral (Ways and Means, Agriculture, Natural Resources, Financial Services, Armed Services)
against.role: Held the bill under simultaneous referral
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 11 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it, and no vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The federal sugar program uses price supports and import restrictions to keep sugar prices above world levels; its benefits flow to sugar growers while the cost is spread across consumers. The bill would have ended that arrangement, and growers kept it because the bill died.
The bill would have ended federal loan guarantees for railroad rehabilitation projects and rail safety research funding, removing federal backing that rail projects rely on.

industries.industry: Regional and local development organizations (EDA/ARC grant recipients)
industries.note: These recipients are not a classic industry, but a concentrated set of local governments and development groups that would have lost federal grant funding for distressed communities.
